description: What the temporal functions DECLARE. The registry names ONE nominal TIMESTAMP_NTZ for the whole family; live answers from the ARGUMENT, and only DATEADD over a DATE consults the UNIT as well - a whole-day unit (day, year, month, week, quarter) leaves a DATE a DATE while a sub-day one (hour and below) promotes it to TIMESTAMP_NTZ. The spelling of the call changes nothing: a quoted unit, a non-constant amount and the TIMEADD / TIMESTAMPADD aliases all follow the same rule. Anything already carrying a time keeps its OWN flavour whatever the unit, TIME included. Truncation never changes the family - not even an hour truncation of a DATE. LAST_DAY and NEXT_DAY always answer a DATE whatever they are handed, while ADD_MONTHS keeps the family. A DIFFERENCE is sized by its unit, and the step sits between HOUR and MINUTE rather than where 'sub-day units are wider' would put it: 9 digits at HOUR and above, 18 from MINUTE down, 38 below a second. A conversion and a part constructor each declare the flavour their OWN NAME asks for, not the one behind it. Among the clock functions CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is the ZONED one and SYSDATE is not. And the base columns are untouched, so none of the rules reach past the functions. Converted 1:1 from query/TemporalResultTypeTest (now retired); the Java read every declared type through the engine's Java DataType API, so each converted claim materialises its expression as a VIEW and reads that view's INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS row - DATETIME_PRECISION carries the temporal precision (NULL for DATE, which renders as the 0 the Java printed) and NUMERIC_PRECISION/SCALE the difference's size.
